_note: Quote of the day: a small card shown once a day, after about 5 minutes on the site in one visit. One item per day (Sri Lanka date), in this order, then from the top again. Fields: quote (exact words; ' / ' marks a line break in poetry), text (title), author, link (the text's page), question (a thoughtful question for students). check-practice.js checks every quote word for word against the texts, and build.js checks every link. Quote copyrighted texts only in short lines. Never quote 'Father and Son' (song lyrics).

items.quote: Yet Love is better than Life
items.author: Oscar Wilde
items.question: Was the Nightingale's sacrifice wise, or foolish? Would the story mean the same if the Student had kept the rose?

items.quote: I have learned to wear many faces / like dresses
items.author: Gabriel Okara
items.question: Do you show a different 'face' at home, at school and with friends? When is that sensible, and when does it become false?

items.quote: The wrinkled sea beneath him crawls
items.author: Alfred, Lord Tennyson
items.question: The mighty sea looks small and 'wrinkled' from the eagle's height. How does where we stand change how big a problem looks?

items.quote: Talking brought me here.
items.author: Edward Lowbury
items.question: When can words be dangerous? Think of a time when saying less would have been wiser.

items.quote: These men were born to drill and die
items.author: Stephen Crane
items.question: Is anyone really 'born' for war? What does Crane want us to feel about the soldiers?

items.quote: It was probably the first time for twenty years that anyone had smiled in that lumber-room.
items.author: Saki
items.question: Why do some people keep beautiful things locked away instead of enjoying them? What does Saki think of that?

items.quote: The caged bird sings of freedom.
items.text: I Know Why the Caged Bird Sings
items.author: Maya Angelou
items.question: Why does the caged bird sing at all? What can people do when they are not free?

items.quote: I do not know you, woman!
items.author: Mark Twain
items.question: Why does Tom deny his own mother? What does his shame afterwards tell us about him?

items.quote: And Richard Cory, one calm summer night, / Went home and put a bullet through his head.
items.author: Edwin Arlington Robinson
items.question: The townspeople thought Richard Cory had everything. Why is it hard to know what others really feel?

items.quote: I don't want them to turn / my little girl into a swallow.
items.author: Gabriela Mistral
items.question: Can love hold a person back? How should parents balance keeping children close and letting them fly?

items.quote: speak silence with thy glimmering eyes, / And wash the dusk with silver.
items.author: William Blake
items.question: How can eyes 'speak silence'? Find another place where Blake mixes the senses in this poem.

items.quote: We were shot at, grenades were thrown at us, we were injured and yet we were not cowed.
items.author: Kumar Sangakkara
items.question: What helps people stay calm and united in danger? Is courage the absence of fear?

items.quote: I'd rather sit on a barrel of gunpowder than talk to a woman.
items.author: Anton Chekhov
items.question: Why are Smirnov's strongest words the funniest by the end of the play? What does Chekhov say about loud opinions?

items.quote: Up there he's a king on a throne, / but at home you should hear him moan.
items.author: John Agard
items.question: Is a person's public face their real one? How can we help someone who hides their sadness?

items.quote: 'Tis ignorance that makes a barren waste / Of all beyond itself
items.author: John Keats
items.question: Do we sometimes think a place or a people is 'barren' only because we don't know them? What changes Keats's mind?

items.quote: No one spoke. No one uttered a sound.
items.author: Sonali Deraniyagala
items.question: Why can silence be more frightening than screams? How does the writer use short sentences here?

items.quote: She had two sons at rising day, / To-night she'll be alone.
items.text: Farewell to Barn and Stack and Tree
items.author: A.E. Housman
items.question: How can one angry moment change a family for ever? Do you feel any sympathy for the speaker?

items.quote: To crack nuts with!
items.author: Mark Twain
items.question: Tom used the Great Seal of England to crack nuts. What does this funny moment say about symbols of power?

items.quote: If he was told to turn to right / He turned to left out of spite.
items.author: Alexander Kushner
items.question: Is it ever right to go against what everyone else does? Should we laugh at Upside-Down or admire him?

items.quote: And he unrolled his feathers / And rowed him softer Home
items.text: A Bird Came Down the Walk
items.author: Emily Dickinson
items.question: Why does Dickinson describe flying as rowing? What other surprising images can you find in the poem?

items.quote: Why–why did you look in at me?
items.author: Junji Kinoshita
items.question: Why is a broken promise so hard to undo? Who is most to blame for Tsu's leaving?

items.quote: the hump we get / From having too little to do
items.author: Rudyard Kipling
items.question: Are you grumpier when you are busy or when you are idle? What is Kipling's 'cure'?

items.quote: What a silly thing Love is
items.author: Oscar Wilde
items.question: The Student calls love 'silly'. Who is really foolish in the story, and why?

items.quote: So show me, son, / how to laugh
items.author: Gabriel Okara
items.question: What can adults learn from children? Why does the father ask his son for help?

items.quote: Gandhi has taught me peaceful methods, and that's how I'm going to meet their demand.
items.author: R.K. Narayan
items.question: Is Jagan really following Gandhi here, or using his ideas to protect his money? Can it be both?

items.quote: I am the ghost. Pray who are you?
items.author: Raymond Wilson
items.question: Why is the ending funny? What does it suggest about people who are too sure of themselves?

items.quote: Kings cannot ennoble thee, thou good, great soul
items.author: Mark Twain
items.question: What makes a person truly noble: birth, wealth, or the way they act? Think of Miles Hendon.

items.quote: And then came the bark; the sharp clipped aristocratic bark
items.author: Tissa Abeysekara
items.question: How can a single sound bring back a memory? Which sounds remind you of your own childhood?

items.quote: How can this man value his life less than mine?
items.author: Kumar Sangakkara
items.question: Why did this question make Sangakkara feel 'humbled'? Is one life worth more than another?

items.quote: With just one flower flaming through my breast
items.author: Harindranath Chattopadhyaya
items.question: What did the clay lose when the potter shaped it into a goblet? Is change always progress?

items.quote: Death is a great price to pay for a red rose
items.author: Oscar Wilde
items.question: The Nightingale knows the price and pays it anyway. What would you be willing to give up for something you believe in?

items.quote: You often don't listen when we tell you important things.
items.author: Saki
items.question: Do adults always listen to children? Is Nicholas right, or just rude?

items.quote: Here the sexes are equal! I'll shoot her on principle!
items.author: Anton Chekhov
items.question: Smirnov talks about equality while challenging a woman to a duel. How does Chekhov make this scene both funny and thought-provoking?

items.quote: Oh my God, the sea's coming in.
items.author: Sonali Deraniyagala
items.question: The first warning sounds almost ordinary. Why do people often fail to see danger until it is too late?

items.quote: Here at last is a true lover
items.author: Oscar Wilde
items.question: The Nightingale decides the Student is a true lover. Is she right? What is a "true lover" in this story?

items.quote: Nicholas was in an unknown land
items.author: Saki
items.question: The lumber-room feels like a new world to Nicholas. Is there a place that felt like an "unknown land" to you?

items.quote: Ah, on what little things does happiness depend!
items.author: Oscar Wilde
items.question: Does your happiness depend on little things? Is the Student's sorrow about the rose real or shallow?

items.quote: She was a woman of few ideas, with immense powers of concentration.
items.author: Saki
items.question: How does this sentence make fun of the aunt? Find another sentence where Saki mocks her.

items.quote: Pearls and pomegranates cannot buy it, nor is it set forth in the marketplace.
items.author: Oscar Wilde
items.question: Can anything truly valuable be bought? Which characters in the story think it can?

items.quote: To Nicholas it was a living, breathing story
items.author: Saki
items.question: A tapestry becomes a story in Nicholas's mind. How does imagination make ordinary things exciting?

items.quote: Love is wiser than Philosophy, though she is wise, and mightier than Power, though he is mighty.
items.author: Oscar Wilde
items.question: Wilde personifies Love, Philosophy and Power. Do you agree that love is stronger than knowledge and power?

items.quote: he felt perfectly capable of being in disgrace and in a gooseberry garden at the same moment
items.author: Saki
items.question: Nicholas spots the flaw in his aunt's reasoning. Was she being fair? Is he being clever or cheeky?

items.quote: she is all style, without any sincerity
items.author: Oscar Wilde
items.question: The Student says this about the Nightingale. Why is it ironic? Who in the story really lacks sincerity?

items.quote: he did not believe in trusting too much to luck and accident
items.author: Saki
items.question: Nicholas practised with the schoolroom key before he tried the lumber-room. What does careful planning have to do with success?

items.quote: I am afraid it will not go with my dress
items.author: Oscar Wilde
items.question: The girl rejects a rose made with a life. What does this tell us about what she values?

items.quote: Tea that evening was partaken of in a fearsome silence.
items.author: Saki
items.question: Everyone is unhappy except Nicholas. Who has really been punished by the end of the day?

items.quote: as in this age to be practical is everything
items.author: Oscar Wilde
items.question: Is being practical everything? What might we lose if we only value what is useful?

items.quote: Oh, Devil, you have sold yourself!
items.author: Saki
items.question: Nicholas turns his aunt's own words against her. Is he wise, or a little cruel?

items.quote: he only knew the things that are written down in books
items.author: Oscar Wilde
items.question: Can someone be well read but still not understand people? What can books not teach?

items.quote: My life is already at an end.
items.author: Anton Chekhov
items.question: Popova says her life is over, yet soon she is in love again. Is her grief real, or partly for show?

items.quote: Would God I were free of my captivity!
items.author: Mark Twain
items.question: Tom wanted to be a prince, but now feels like a captive. Can wealth and power be a prison?

items.quote: Beauty won't last long, you know.
items.author: Anton Chekhov
items.question: Luka urges Popova to enjoy life. Is he wise or just practical? What would you tell her?

items.quote: Wouldst sit in the presence of the King?
items.author: Mark Twain
items.question: The ragged boy still acts like a king. Is Edward proud, or simply true to who he is?

items.quote: I'm weak, I'm wax, I've melted
items.author: Anton Chekhov
items.question: The "bear" has become wax. How does Chekhov use this sudden change to make us laugh?

items.quote: Royalty had lost its grace and sweetness; its pomps were become a reproach.
items.author: Mark Twain
items.question: Why does the splendour suddenly feel like a reproach to Tom? What has he learned?

items.quote: I'm in love like a boy, like a fool!
items.author: Anton Chekhov
items.question: Smirnov swore he would never love again. Why do people often change their strongest opinions?

items.quote: It is argument that other mothers are made in like mould.
items.author: Mark Twain
items.question: Tom uses his love for his own mother to judge fairly. Can our own experiences make us kinder judges?

items.quote: Fallen into a mousetrap, like a mouse!
items.author: Anton Chekhov
items.question: Who has trapped whom in this play? Is love a trap, or a release?

items.quote: Remorse was eating his heart out.
items.author: Mark Twain
items.question: Tom feels deep remorse. Why is a guilty conscience a sign of a good person?

items.quote: You'll meet a cat with a horn or a white woodcock sooner than a constant woman!
items.author: Anton Chekhov
items.question: Smirnov uses exaggeration to insult women. How does the rest of the play prove him wrong?

items.quote: Edward of England dubs thee Earl!
items.author: Mark Twain
items.question: Edward rewards Hendon's loyalty in the stocks. What makes Hendon worthy of this honour?

items.quote: Not a sour-faced jellybag, but fire, gunpowder, a rocket!
items.author: Anton Chekhov
items.question: What qualities does Smirnov suddenly admire in Popova? Why does her courage change his mind?

items.quote: Son of the old moon-mountains African!
items.author: John Keats
items.question: Keats speaks to the river as if it were a person. Why do poets personify nature?

items.quote: I am not here as a visitor, but as a creditor
items.author: Anton Chekhov
items.question: Smirnov came for money and leaves with love. What does the play suggest about plans and feelings?

items.quote: Chief of the Pyramid and Crocodile!
items.author: John Keats
items.question: Why might the Nile be called the "Chief" of the pyramids and crocodiles? What does it give to the land?

items.quote: Thou fair-hair'd angel of the evening
items.author: William Blake
items.question: Blake turns a star into an angel. How does this image set the mood of the poem?

items.quote: O may dark fancies err! They surely do
items.author: John Keats
items.question: Here the poem turns. What "dark fancies" does Keats reject, and why?

items.quote: then the wolf rages wide, / And then the lion glares through the dun forest
items.author: William Blake
items.question: When the star goes, danger comes. What might the star, the wolf and the lion stand for?

items.quote: They looked like frightened Beads, I thought
items.text: A Bird Came Down the Walk
items.author: Emily Dickinson
items.question: Why "frightened Beads"? How does the bird feel about the speaker?

items.quote: He clasps the crag with crooked hands
items.author: Alfred, Lord Tennyson
items.question: Count the hard "c" sounds. What do they tell us about the eagle?

items.quote: He bit an Angle Worm in halves / And ate the fellow, raw
items.text: A Bird Came Down the Walk
items.author: Emily Dickinson
items.question: Nature is beautiful and cruel in the same poem. Why does Dickinson show both?

items.quote: And like a thunderbolt he falls.
items.author: Alfred, Lord Tennyson
items.question: Why end the poem on this sudden movement? What might the eagle be diving for?

items.quote: Do not weep, maiden, for war is kind.
items.author: Stephen Crane
items.question: Is war kind? Why does Crane say the opposite of what he means?

items.quote: Farewell to barn and stack and tree, / Farewell to Severn shore.
items.text: Farewell to Barn and Stack and Tree
items.author: A.E. Housman
items.question: The speaker says goodbye to his home. Why is a farewell to ordinary things so moving?

items.quote: A field where a thousand corpses lie.
items.author: Stephen Crane
items.question: Crane shows the "kingdom" of the battle-god. How does this image answer the idea of glory?

items.quote: And here's a bloody hand to shake
items.text: Farewell to Barn and Stack and Tree
items.author: A.E. Housman
items.question: A handshake usually means friendship. What does this bloody hand mean instead?

items.quote: Mother whose heart hung humble as a button / On the bright splendid shroud of your son
items.author: Stephen Crane
items.question: Why compare a mother's heart to a button? What does "bright splendid shroud" suggest?

items.quote: We people on the pavement looked at him
items.author: Edwin Arlington Robinson
items.question: The poem is told by "we", the ordinary people. How does their point of view shape the story?

items.quote: But a caged bird stands on the grave of dreams
items.text: I Know Why the Caged Bird Sings
items.author: Maya Angelou
items.question: What are the "dreams" of the caged bird? Who might the caged bird stand for?

items.quote: So on we worked, and waited for the light, / And went without the meat, and cursed the bread
items.author: Edwin Arlington Robinson
items.question: The townspeople envy Richard Cory. Were they really worse off than him?

items.quote: A free bird leaps on the back / Of the wind
items.text: I Know Why the Caged Bird Sings
items.author: Maya Angelou
items.question: How does Angelou make freedom feel easy and joyful? Why does she contrast it with the cage?

items.quote: but now they only laugh with their teeth
items.author: Gabriel Okara
items.question: What is the difference between laughing with your heart and laughing with your teeth?

items.quote: His wings are clipped and his feet are tied / So he opens his throat to sing.
items.text: I Know Why the Caged Bird Sings
items.author: Maya Angelou
items.question: When the body is trapped, the voice is still free. What can people do when their freedom is taken away?

items.quote: for then I find doors shut on me.
items.author: Gabriel Okara
items.question: "Come again," people say, but the doors are shut. Have you seen friendliness that was not real?

items.quote: They would put her on a throne / where I could not go to see her.
items.author: Gabriela Mistral
items.question: Why does the mother fear success as much as danger? What does the throne stand for?

items.quote: I want to unlearn all these muting things.
items.author: Gabriel Okara
items.question: What are the "muting things" the father wants to unlearn? Can adults change?

items.quote: In tiny golden slippers / how could she play on the meadow?
items.author: Gabriela Mistral
items.question: Can wealth take away simple joys? What would the girl lose as a princess?

items.quote: I do me best to cheer him up, poor soul.
items.author: John Agard
items.question: Who is really the clown in this marriage? How does the wife show her love?

items.quote: The cure for this ill is not to sit still
items.author: Rudyard Kipling
items.question: Kipling's cure for a bad mood is work. Do you agree? What helps you when you feel low?

items.quote: what would I do without this clown of a wife?
items.author: John Agard
items.question: The clown calls his wife "this clown of a wife". Is it an insult or a compliment?

items.quote: And dig till you gently perspire
items.author: Rudyard Kipling
items.question: Why "gently"? How does Kipling make hard work sound pleasant?

items.quote: But he doesn't say exactly how he feels
items.author: John Agard
items.question: Why do some people hide their feelings even from those who love them?

items.quote: He read his letters backside-fore
items.author: Alexander Kushner
items.question: How does the poet make a silly character so memorable? Find a technique in this line.

items.quote: Never since I was born of my mother / Have I seen or heard of a skull which spoke.
items.author: Edward Lowbury
items.question: The king does not believe Kagwa. Should he have trusted him? What would you have done?

items.quote: Was funnier than the circus clown
items.author: Alexander Kushner
items.question: People laugh at Upside-Down. Is the laughter kind or cruel? What does the poem suggest?

items.quote: The skull said nothing.
items.author: Edward Lowbury
items.question: Why does the skull stay silent in front of the guards? Is it fate, a trick, or a lesson?

items.quote: Shall I read it? P'raps I ought, / P'raps I will, p'raps I can't.
items.author: Alexander Kushner
items.question: Upside-Down cannot decide. Why is indecision both funny and frustrating?

items.quote: knowing it's every sane man's mission / to contradict all superstition
items.author: Raymond Wilson
items.question: The man is proud of being sensible. How does the poem show that pride comes before a fall?

items.quote: Flash point in Paradise.
items.author: Yasmine Gooneratne
items.question: Why use a newspaper headline in a poem? What does "Paradise" make you think of Sri Lanka?

items.quote: (but just the same, he draws the curtain)
items.author: Raymond Wilson
items.question: The brackets show what he really does. Why are the brackets so funny?

items.quote: a minority with a majority complex
items.author: Yasmine Gooneratne
items.question: What might this phrase mean? Why can fear of the "other" grow on both sides of a conflict?

items.quote: with a hunchback moon and screech owls calling
items.author: Raymond Wilson
items.question: How does this line build a spooky atmosphere? Name the sounds and images.

items.quote: I felt a conscious impulse in my clay, to break away
items.author: Harindranath Chattopadhyaya
items.question: The clay wanted to escape the potter. Do we sometimes resist being shaped by others?

items.quote: There was absolute clarity and awareness of what was happening at that moment.
items.author: Kumar Sangakkara
items.question: In great danger, Sangakkara felt clear and calm. How can people stay calm in a crisis?

items.quote: But I didn't know what I was fleeing from
items.author: Sonali Deraniyagala
items.question: The narrator runs before she understands. Why do we sometimes act on instinct before thinking?

items.quote: Our emotions held true to our role as unofficial ambassadors.
items.author: Kumar Sangakkara
items.question: The players felt they represented Sri Lanka even in danger. What does it mean to represent your country?

items.quote: white curl of a big wave
items.author: Sonali Deraniyagala
items.question: The first sight of the wave seems harmless, even pretty. Why does that make the extract more tragic?

items.quote: Within minutes there is laughter and the jokes have started to flow.
items.author: Kumar Sangakkara
items.question: Why do people laugh after a frightening experience? How does humour help a team?

items.quote: But I had another very important task to perform, something I had secretly vowed to myself I would do.
items.author: Tissa Abeysekara
items.question: What secret vow does the boy keep? What makes a promise to yourself important?

items.quote: Gradually his reading of the Bhagavad Gita was replaced by the blue airmail letters.
items.author: R.K. Narayan
items.question: What has replaced Jagan's holy book? What does this show about his love for his son?

items.quote: having broken through classroom order there is no wish to get back to it
items.author: Tissa Abeysekara
items.question: Why is it so hard to calm a class once it is laughing? What does the scene show about the narrator?

items.quote: at some stage in one's life one must uproot oneself from the accustomed surroundings and disappear so that others may continue in peace.
items.author: R.K. Narayan
items.question: Is Jagan's wish to leave wise, or is he running away from his problems?

items.quote: I wished I might have lived with you forever
items.author: Junji Kinoshita
items.question: Tsu wanted a simple life with Yohyo. What destroyed that dream: greed, broken trust, or both?

items.quote: He should rather go to a village granny
items.author: R.K. Narayan
items.question: Jagan thinks stories belong to village grandmothers, not American classes. Who is right, Jagan or Mali?

items.quote: it's very nice to have got two pieces of the cloth
items.author: Junji Kinoshita
items.question: Tsu has just left, yet this speaker thinks only of the cloth. What does that show about greed?

items.quote: he goes back in for his crummy gloves
items.author: Wislawa Szymborska
items.question: A small decision may decide whether this man lives. How does the poet show the role of chance?
